Then there are clients who want AI in everything. I like the energy, but I always slow it down.
 
Fast adoption goes wrong the same way every time. The output sounds so confident that people stop checking it. Then it gets something wrong, and nobody trusts it again. So I pick one job first, run it for a couple of weeks, and see if it actually saves time before touching anything else.
 
First I ask whether a rule can do it. If the input is a form field, a number, a date or a known keyword, rules do it better. They’re cheaper, they’re exact, and you can see why they did what they did. I only bring in AI when the input is messy, and the meaning has to be understood.
 
That looks like this:
- Summarising a long email thread or document so someone can catch up in a minute
- Drafting a first reply in the right tone, which a person reads and edits
- Reading scanned or photographed documents and invoices and turning them into data
- Working out what an email is asking for when it doesn’t follow any pattern
- Searching your files by meaning, like “the contract where we agreed the late fee”
- Pulling details out of free text where the layout is different every time
 
Where it struggles: exact facts like figures, dates and references, unusual cases it hasn’t seen, and decisions that need someone responsible, because a model can’t be.
 
So I put AI on top of rules, not instead of them. The rules do the parts that must be exact, like deadlines, invoices and approvals. The AI handles the messy reading and drafting. A person checks anything that matters before it goes out.
A generic chatbot also doesn’t know your business. A custom setup uses your own records and your rules, but it costs more, and the cost doesn’t stop at the build. There are usage fees, monitoring and fixes.
 
The upside is real: time saved on repetitive work, and more capacity without hiring at the same pace. The downside is output that needs checking, running costs, and people trusting it too much.
AI speeds up a process that already works. If your process is a mess, you just get the mess faster.

🚀 API Testing – What Should a Manual Tester Validate?
Many testers think API testing is just sending a request and checking whether the status code is 200 OK.


But API testing goes beyond that!
As a Manual Tester, here are the important validations I always consider:
✅ Status Code – Is the API returning the correct status code?
✅ Response Body – Are all expected fields present?
✅ Data Accuracy – Are the returned values correct?
✅ Headers – Are the required headers available?
✅ Schema Validation – Are the field names and data types correct?
✅ Error Handling – Does the API handle invalid inputs properly?
✅ Response Time – Does the API meet performance expectations?
✅ Authentication & Authorization – Can only authorized users access the data?
✅ Boundary Testing – What happens with null, empty, minimum and maximum values?

💡 Real-time example:
API: GET /users/123
Expected validations:
Status code: 200 OK
User ID should be 123
Name and email should be returned correctly
Response structure should match the API contract
Response time should meet the agreed SLA

If the user doesn't exist, the API should return the expected error response, such as 404 Not Found.

Remember: A 200 OK response doesn't always mean the API is working correctly!
Test the response, validate the data, and verify the business logic.
Happy Testing! 💻

Spent this morning with Matt Knowles from NorthStar People and we kept coming back to the same thing. The hardest roles I’m trying to fill in MedTech AI right now aren’t really roles at all, they’re combinations.

There are plenty of good ML engineers and plenty of good regulatory people. What there isn’t is enough people who are properly both.

Day to day, the profiles everyone wants and almost nobody can find look something like this:

AI regulatory affairs: Someone who knows MDR and IVDR inside out and can now hold their own on the EU AI Act, model validation and algorithm change control without treating them as separate jobs.
SaMD engineers: Software people who build to IEC 62304 and understand that a model that looks brilliant on a benchmark still has to survive a technical file.
Clinical AI: Clinicians with real ML literacy, or engineers who’ve spent years inside clinical product teams and can tell you whether it actually works on a ward and own clinical safety when it goes live.
MLOps, regulated: Anyone can deploy a model; deploying one you can trace, document and monitor for drift with a notified body watching is different.
AI and cyber in one head: Securing clinical systems and governing AI risk at the same time — most org charts haven’t got a title for it yet.

Plenty of candidates have two of those boxes ticked, a few have three, and the ones with everything are being chased by MedTech, big tech and well-funded scale-ups.

That’s why this can’t be done off a keyword search and a pile of CVs. You have to spot who’s 70% there and know which 30% can be built around them. Sometimes the answer is two people who cover each other’s gaps, or a contract specialist bridging the AI Act piece while the team grows into it.

So, I’m genuinely curious: whether you’re hiring in MedTech or you’re one of these rare people yourself, which profile is the hardest to find right now, and is it a real shortage, or is the industry just asking for unicorns?

Frasca Executive Dispatch | Wednesday: AI (Enterprise / Leadership)

The AI budget has quietly become a labor budget. I have built AI companies since the 1990s. In every wave, the technology arrived first and the cost discipline arrived late. Three items this week put the cost question on the CFO's desk.

1. On 10 November, OpenAI's Greg Brockman announced that JPMorganChase signed a contract to use Codex agents to write, review, debug and ship code, per American Banker. CFO Jeremy Barnum said last month the bank spends "something like $700 million annually" on AI, and cited token costs as an offset to the benefits.

2. Also on 10 November, Reuters reported McKinsey's Global Banking Annual Review: token spending for AI agents "could easily reach 20% of total labor costs." Senior partner Vik Sohoni said routing staff to cheaper models stops working once agents talk to each other.

3. On 9 November, Fortune reported an SHL survey: 19.1% of US respondents said they were replaced by AI and later asked back. A separate Robert Half survey found 32% of US hiring managers who cut roles because of AI later reinstated them. Of those, 40% cited institutional knowledge AI could not replace.

What this rhymes with: early cloud. The bills arrived before the operating model did.

Second-order effect: agents are now a variable labor cost with no headcount line. Firms that cut people first can end up paying twice, once in tokens and once to rehire.

For institutions: budget agents like headcount. Name an owner, a unit cost and a reversal plan before a role is removed.

AI doesn't replace experience. It compresses it.

— Rob Frasca | COSIMO Digital | cosimodigital.com

“Skills over headcount” is the polite way of saying “we’d rather not train anyone anymore.”

India’s GCCs are one of the country’s biggest talent success stories. And rightly so.

But look at who they are hiring now.

foundit’s data shows the entry-level share of GCC hiring has dropped from 42% to 30%. Professionals with four to six years of experience have gone from 26% to 34%. And GCCs are reportedly offering up to a 40% salary premium for AI talent (Storyboard18).

So the pay is going up, and the door is getting narrower.

Business Today reports they are also hiring fewer full-timers and more AI contractors, breaking one broad role into specific skills brought in as needed.

On paper, this is smart. Lean teams, precise skills, faster output.

But here’s where it gets interesting.

What does a 22-year-old hear? Be skilled before anyone gives you the chance to learn.

If the entry-level role keeps shrinking, how does anyone become a senior hire? If every role is a rented skill, who holds the knowledge when the contract ends?

Companies call it capability. A fresher calls it a locked door.

Every organisation wants senior talent. Very few want to be the place that builds it.

I actually think this is one of the more uncomfortable questions in talent strategy right now. The answer isn’t to go back to mass hiring. It’s to be honest about who pays for learning when nobody wants to.

Curious how founders, CEOs and talent leaders see this.

Is skills-first hiring the smartest shift in years, or a way of outsourcing the cost of learning to everyone else?

Budgets are being signed off. Headcount plans are being locked in. And the best tech contractors are already lining up their January start dates before the Christmas lights go up.

It makes sense. AI infrastructure, hybrid cloud and security programmes are moving faster than org charts can keep up. Businesses want proven skills on the project, not fixed headcount on the payroll while the roadmap is still settling.

→ Line up your shortlist early. Nobody wants to start the year interviewing from scratch.

Executive search sounds expensive, and terms differ from firm to firm.
But for hard roles it pays off: when the right person barely exists on the market, and the few who do aren't job hunting or replying to postings, standard recruiting simply doesn't work.

What does that look like in practice?

A startup called 42 came to us. They build autonomous AI agents for HFT research, and needed an architect to design an agent system covering the full research cycle: from generating hypotheses to testing and launch. There's no ready-made playbook for a role like this, and people with real experience building autonomous research agents are rare.

What worked wasn't a flood of applications, but an accumulated pipeline: we'd already run searches for this client, and our recruiter Valeriya Soboleva reviewed those profiles against the new role. One candidate had built a co-scientist system for processing hypotheses and had trading experience. A couple of interviews with the CPO and founder, and an offer.

📎 Read the full case here: https://lnkd.in/eUW5i85B

That's the essence of retained search: we start not from the vacancy but from the market, we see its boundaries and understand what's realistically possible on role, timeline and compensation before the search even begins. Our value isn't access to candidates, it's knowing what will actually work in a specific context.

But an expensive model doesn't guarantee the result on its own: payment structure, guarantees, interview speed and handling counteroffers matter as much as the search itself. A lot here depends on both sides, so we work as partners: we align on expectations, keep the process transparent and get to the offer together.

How this process works step by step, when retained search truly pays off, and what to check in the contract, we broke it all down in the article. Link in the comments 👇

California's school districts are changing superintendents at a pace that should worry every board member, and the numbers now confirm it is not a blip.

In the 2024-25 school year, 18.9 percent of California school districts changed superintendents, up from 11.8 percent before the pandemic. Nationally the rate reached 17.1 percent. In Sonoma County, nearly one in four districts, 9 of 38, turned over their chief this year. A study of the country's 500 largest districts found 23 percent had at least one leadership change in 2024-25. Researchers at The Superintendent Lab now call leadership churn the new normal.

Los Angeles Unified is the sharpest example of what churn costs. Alberto Carvalho resigned in June amid an FBI investigation tied to a 6.2 million dollar AI chatbot contract, after being placed on paid administrative leave in February. Acting Superintendent Andres Chait leads the nation's second largest district while the board has set no timeline for a permanent replacement, and the district is losing two academic chiefs at the same time. It also faces budget deficits and declining enrollment.

The research is blunt about the damage. USC professor Julie Marsh notes that when turnover hits, a new leader may shift priorities or stop reforms, which lowers staff morale and disrupts programs and policies. Continuity is not a luxury in a district. It is the condition that lets a multi-year improvement plan survive long enough to work.

Some boards are responding with a different hiring instinct. West Contra Costa Unified turned to Cheryl Cotton, a homegrown leader who grew up in the district and served five years as a deputy superintendent at the state Department of Education. She arrived with a 100-day plan, "Building a Stronger WCCUSD," that names the district's real problems, declining enrollment, budget deficits, and inconsistent academic outcomes, in plain language. Boards are increasingly betting that a leader who already knows the community can hold the line where an outsider would need a year to learn it.

The leadership lesson here is about systems, not personalities. A board that treats the superintendency as a single hire will keep reliving the same crisis. A board that builds a pipeline, documents its priorities, and keeps reforms alive through a transition is doing the work that actually protects students from churn.

If your district has lived through a leadership change in the last two years, what held steady, and what fell apart first?

Apparently, “buy local” doesn’t extend to hiring. 🦘🦘🦘  🐨🐨 🐨    

Qantas and NAB have announced 3,350 job cuts between them. Coles Group, Woolworths Group and Officeworks have also announced offshoring plans. The reasons vary, but the uncertainty for workers is very real.

My LinkedIn feed is filling with “Open to Work” banners, including people I know personally who are exceptional at what they do.

“Our people are our greatest asset.”
Terms and conditions apply: *until we find a cheaper option.

I support AI and innovation. But cutting local jobs while chasing bigger margins shouldn’t automatically qualify as “transformation”. Sometimes corporate greed just has a nicer slide deck.

The Australian Government needs to do more: require transparency on offshoring, attach stronger local employment expectations to government contracts, and encourage genuine retraining before redundancy.

If Australian customers help build your profits, Australian workers deserve investment too.

After all, the jobs might move overseas, but the bills have a strict work-from-home policy.

And yes, I used AI to help write this. It improved the wording. Somehow, we managed that without announcing a restructure.

Companies want to grow. But does growth always mean hiring more people?
In the first post, we explored India's economic growth and its relationship with employment.

In the second, we looked at how hiring demand is evolving across IT and Non-IT sectors.
There is another important dimension to this discussion: The changing economics of hiring.

Today, organisations are balancing growth ambitions with cost discipline, productivity and profitability.
This is changing how workforce decisions are made.

A few shifts are becoming increasingly visible:

1. Hiring for critical roles
Companies are becoming more selective, prioritising roles that directly contribute to business outcomes.

2. Productivity over headcount
Automation, AI and digital tools are changing how organisations evaluate workforce requirements.

3. Flexible workforce models
Contract staffing, outsourced operations and project-based talent are becoming important considerations for businesses managing variable demand.

4. Workforce rationalisation
Organisations are reviewing structures, eliminating duplication and aligning talent with actual business priorities.

This does not mean hiring is becoming less important.
It means the business case for every hiring decision is becoming more important.

A workforce strategy today must consider not just how many people an organisation needs, but also which capabilities it needs, where it needs them and how quickly those capabilities can be deployed.

A question for CEOs, CFOs and CHROs:
Is the future of recruitment about hiring more people, or creating greater productivity and business value from the workforce we already have?

A difficult UK economy can give businesses a reason to change their leadership, not just freeze recruitment.

There are reports of renewed momentum in UK executive hiring despite economic challenges. That does not prove the economy is causing an increase, but it raises an important distinction: recruiting more leaders and recruiting a different kind of leader are not the same thing.

For CEO, MD and COO appointments, we have noticed a "human" centred shift in the brief recently to combine strong commercial acumen with a genuinely human-centred approach.

That means someone who understands margins, cash flow and growth, but also spends time with employees, listens to clients and customers, and acts on what they hear.

Those are not competing priorities. A customer conversation can expose a service problem before it becomes a lost contract. Customers, Clients and Employees are looking to Executive Leadership to inspire, engage, trust and lead. Listening to and hearing what employees and customers/clients are saying can reveal that 1% of difference that delivers longer term commercial value and success.

With the speed and advancement of technology and tech innovation/AI, we are starting to realise what skills/behaviours are important and it always comes back to human connection with tech enabled efficiency. 

From a Search perspective, the assessment needs to test both sides. Alongside the standard sales/commercial and revenue we need to think deeper and get "under the bonnet" of the people we meet.

At Disrupt we refer to "People Architecture" and see this as a key component of any Search or recruitment process.  

Emotional intelligence and the ability to adapt to your environment is now a non-negotiable to long term survival. Without this how can we win the hearts and minds of the people to put in the hard work so we can all thrive? 

So how are Boards, Co-founders and Executive leadership assessing this?

Are you going beyond the standard questions at interview stage or just recycling the process created in the 1980's?

Truly understanding the people that you are trusting to lead your business should not be underestimated; ask candidates for evidence of how they handled difficult decisions, retained trust, transformed engagement, and test how they received feedback and altered their course for success. 

The strongest appointment should not require a choice between commercial discipline or human engagement. The brief should demand evidence of both.

If AI cuts the hours needed to deliver a project, what should an IT services company charge for?

That question sits at the center of Business Standard's "The great IT reset" article. India's $315 billion IT services industry, employing nearly 6 million people, is rethinking how it delivers work and earns revenue.

AI is taking on coding, testing, documentation and routine maintenance. Clients increasingly expect those productivity gains to translate into better business results.

As Mphasis CEO Nitin Rakesh puts it: "Clients are beginning to move away from buying capacity and inputs, to buying outcomes."

Hiring is changing too. Citing nasscom, the article reports that net employee additions fell nearly 70%, from 445,000 in FY22 to 135,000 in FY26. Annual fresher recruitment has dropped from roughly 380,000 at its post-pandemic peak to about 180,000.

The pricing challenge is immediate. UnearthInsight estimates that some engagements already require 20 - 25% less work. Under contracts based on billable hours, greater productivity can mean lower revenue for the provider.

Coforge is experimenting with fixed-price, subscription and gain-sharing arrangements, using cost, cycle time, quality and risk as starting measures. Yet only around 6 - 7% of its revenue is currently outcome-based. The transition is still underway.

There is new work to build. Enterprises need help preparing data, modernising legacy systems and integrating AI agents into processes, with people accountable for architecture, exceptions and oversight.

Coforge's human-agent operating models and Forward Deployed Engineering unit reflect this direction. Mphasis is pursuing governed AI embedded in business operations, where success could mean faster loan approvals or lower inventory costs.

Talent and location decisions will shift with it. Gaurav Vasu of UnearthInsight says: "The new differentiators are domain expertise, data, and specialisation." Agent reliability remains a concern, alongside security and governance.

The opportunity is substantial: the article cites Nandan Nilekani's estimate of a $300 - 400 billion AI-first services market through 2030. Capturing it will require reusable technology and industry expertise.

What business outcome should your next technology engagement be measured against?

Source: Business Standard | Shelley Singh

A difficult UK economy can give businesses a reason to change their leadership, not just freeze recruitment.

There are reports of renewed momentum in UK executive hiring despite economic challenges. That does not prove the economy is causing an increase, but it raises an important distinction: recruiting more leaders and recruiting a different kind of leader are not the same thing.

For CEO, MD and COO appointments, we have noticed a "human" centred shift in the brief recently to combine strong commercial acumen with a genuinely human-centred approach.

That means someone who understands margins, cash flow and growth, but also spends time with employees, listens to clients and customers, and acts on what they hear.

Those are not competing priorities. A customer conversation can expose a service problem before it becomes a lost contract. Customers, Clients and Employees are looking to Executive Leadership to inspire, engage, trust and lead. Listening to and hearing what employees and customers/clients are saying can reveal that 1% of difference that can make the difference to longer term commercial value.

With the speed and advancement of technology and tech innovation/AI, we are starting to realise what skills/behaviours are important and it always comes back to human connection with tech enabled efficiency. 

From a Search perspective, the assessment needs to test both sides. Alongside the standard sales/commercial and revenue we need to think deeper and get "under the bonnet" of the people we meet.

At Disrupt we refer to "People Architecture" and see this as a key component of any Search or recruitment process.  

Emotional intelligence and the ability to adapt to your environment is now a non-negotiable to long term survival. Without this how can we win the hearts and minds of the people to put in the hard work so we can all thrive? 

So how are Boards, Co-founders and Executive leadership assessing this?

Are you going beyond the standard questions at interview stage or just recycling the process created in the 1980's?

Truly understanding the people that you are trusting to lead your business should noit be underestimated; ask candidates for evidence of how they handled difficult decisions, retained trust, transformed engagement, and test how they received feedback and altered their course for success? 

The strongest appointment should not require a choice between commercial discipline or human engagement. The brief should demand evidence of both.

Why Tech Doesn’t Need an Army of Builders Anymore.

Everyone blames AI for taking tech jobs, but that’s not the whole story. What’s actually happening comes down to two simple things: companies overhired for a hype wave they’re losing, and their core apps just don’t need as many people anymore.

Look at the AI race. Big tech firms poured tons of money into hiring thousands of engineers to build their own AI tools so they wouldn't fall behind. In practice, most regular people and developers keep using ChatGPT or Claude. The big corporations realized they blew massive budgets trying to force their own versions, and now that they aren't winning the market, they're cutting those bloated teams. When those projects get dialed back, the outsourced work and support contracts tied to them dry up too.

The other piece is that software simply grows up. Think about any major food delivery or ride-share app. When teams were building them from scratch, they needed hundreds of developers working round the clock to get map tracking right, hook up payments, and build separate apps for iPhone and Android.

Fast forward a few years. The app works, the bugs are ironed out, and the system is stable. Keeping the lights on and tweaking a few settings takes a small crew, not an army. Why keep paying hundreds of developers high salaries to maintain something that is already built?

AI might slowly chip away at repetitive tasks over time, but the layoffs right now aren't some sci-fi robot takeover. Companies simply built what they needed, wasted money on projects that didn't pan out, and are now trimming the excess.

👉America added 337,000 lawyers, accountants, developers and analysts since ChatGPT. Only about 2,000 went to a law firm, accounting firm, software house or consultancy.

That's from a new Brookings paper by Luis Garicano (LSE).

→ Those four occupations grew 2.5% a year from 2022 to 2025 → 𝟵𝟵% 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘄 𝗷𝗼𝗯𝘀 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘀𝘁 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝗺𝘀 → Professional-services employment grew 0.5% a year since late 2022, against 2.6% in the 2010s

The specialists didn't disappear. They changed employer.

His mechanism: a specialist's edge is learning something once and selling it to many clients. AI makes that knowledge cheap, and cheap knowledge helps the occasional user most. That's the client.

So frequent, easy-to-check work moves in-house: routine contracts, bookkeeping, code.

Rare, hard-to-check work stays with specialists: the one-off merger, the restructuring, the first senior hire.

(His caveat, not mine: early evidence consistent with the mechanism, not proof of cause.)

Make the frequent work in-house. Buy the rare work.

If your US launch plan is a law firm, a payroll provider and three agencies, it was built for the old model.

After a little break, I'm continuing to chronicle each of my five years freelancing with more transparency than I've shown before. This is YEAR THREE. The bad year. Links to the others in the comments.

Year Three is the year ChatGPT comes out. I lose three clients almost overnight. I sympathise with the creative agencies; they're losing work too. The others say it's nothing to do with AI. Sure. I have bits here and there, but it’s not enough to sustain me. 

I begrudgingly get certified with a number of AI tools and spend a hideous amount of time applying to jobs. After a few months of bleakness, I am ready to leave freelancing. I open up my search to part-time and full-time. 

Within months of this revolutionary technology hitting the market, I am asked to summarise what the rise in generative AI means for content and SEO in a 30-second, one-way interview. They create a brand detractor for life. Still, it's an insight into the pressures on writers and marketers to have it figured out with little data. 

After six months, I get a full-time offer I’m really excited about. I provisionally accept, but they're hit by a hiring freeze the day I’m supposed to receive my contract.

I do some extra-ing on movie sets, something I've always enjoyed but that is not stable. I look after friends’ dogs to get out of the house. I exercise a lot, but then break my ankle. My mental health takes a nose dive. I only realise later that in the fog, I did not ask a single person for help. 

I write articles in a few magazines, and the pay is often shockingly low. I get offered a couple of gigs to train AI models to write better. I’m desperate, but I reject them. I explain that while I’m not naive enough to think AI won’t change everything, I'm also not going to build systems that help kill a craft I love. I also turn down offers to edit hundreds of thousands of AI-generated words for under minimum wage.

I direct most of my energy to AI upskilling and build a website called Stubborn Travel. I run SEO experiments on content that is human vs. AI-generated vs. AI-assisted. I’m depressed that this seems to be my new path, but feel I need to future-proof myself.

At the end of the year, the tides begin to turn. People start to notice that while AI can generate a lot of content, people don't like that content. I pick up two huge clients, both through freelance marketplaces. While my skills kept them as clients, I believe landing them was total luck. Luck for being in the right place at the right time, and luck in a way, for having so few bookings that I could start immediately as they both required.

I work a crazy amount the final months. I'm overbooked, working evenings, weekends, everything. Turning down clients. I'm stressed but so grateful. Thanks to these months, my income Year 3 was the same as Year 1 and 2, or around 20% less than my former full-time job. If you just looked at the numbers, you'd think I'd had three years of smooth sailing.

Year 4 and 5 coming soon.

A job posting reads differently once you check the contract type, and this one matters.
United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) lists the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Innovation Analyst position or role at International Personnel Services Agreement-9 (IPSA-9), based in Bonn, open to internal and external applicants, with a deadline of 24th November 2026. One guide gives the reference as #38011, in the Bureau for Management Services, a one(1)-year full-time contract, with a Master’s degree or Bachelor’s degree and two (2) to four (4) years of professional experience depending on education, English required and French or Spanish desirable, and the deadline as 25th November 2026. The one(1)-day difference reflects time zones, and United Nations Development Programme's (UNDP’s) own date is the safer one to plan around. Because the contract is a personnel agreement and not a staff appointment, benefits and entitlements differ, so read the vacancy terms before assuming “United Nations (UN) salary and benefits.” 
For anyone building a career in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and development, the position or role is not alone. United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF) is hiring an Information Technology (IT) Analyst for Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Emerging Technologies in New York at the same grade, and the Digital, Artificial Intelligence (AI) & Innovation Hub has a home-based Data & Artificial Intelligence (AI) Project Analyst opening. Bonn also continues United Nations Development Programme's (UNDP’s) move of capacity to the city, as we earlier discussed. Combined with the other digital-hiring announcements, United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) appears to be investing in Artificial Intelligence (AI) capacity across several locations at once.
